course.title: Threat Intelligence
course.description: A vendor-neutral, research-backed course in cyber threat intelligence that teaches students how to turn threat information into defensible decisions. It covers intelligence requirements and lifecycle management; source evaluation; indicators and observables; enrichment; confidence and freshness; STIX 2.1 and TAXII 2.1; TLP 2.0; MISP and OpenCTI concepts; ATT&CK-based behavioral context; infrastructure and campaign clustering; hypothesis testing; vulnerability intelligence; operationalization into detection and threat hunting; controlled sharing; governance; metrics; feed-risk management; and incident-response feedback. The capstone is an auditable local Python CTI fusion pipeline using synthetic training data. The course is designed for cybersecurity learners and junior-to-intermediate CTI/SOC practitioners who want strong vendor-neutral practical foundations.
prerequisites: Basic networking concepts including IP addressing, DNS, and HTTP/HTTPS
Basic cybersecurity concepts including assets, vulnerabilities, incidents, and common threat terminology
Ability to read and modify simple Python 3 code
Python 3.11+ for the practical labs and capstone
learningOutcomes: define intelligence requirements and align collection to decisions
evaluate CTI sources using explicit reliability, relevance, timeliness, precision, coverage, and operational criteria
classify, normalize, enrich, deduplicate, age, and prioritize indicators
construct and explain core STIX 2.1 objects and relationships
describe TAXII 2.1 exchange concepts and operational security considerations
apply TLP 2.0 handling labels and distinguish handling from access control
map observed behavior to MITRE ATT&CK with explicit evidence and uncertainty
cluster infrastructure and campaigns without over-claiming attribution
construct competing hypotheses and document confidence
translate intelligence into threat-hunting and detection requirements
design sharing-ready intelligence products with provenance and feedback
apply CTI governance, quality assurance, source-risk, and incident-feedback practices
build and test an auditable local CTI fusion pipeline

modules.title: Threat Intelligence Foundations
modules.description: Build the decision-oriented mindset, lifecycle, vocabulary, and source discipline needed for intelligence work.

lessons.title: Threat Intelligence as Decision Support
lessons.description: Establish what cyber threat intelligence is, what it is not, and why intelligence products must be tied to decisions.
learningObjectives: distinguish data, information, indicators, intelligence, and decisions
identify tactical, operational, and strategic consumers
explain why context, provenance, confidence, and timeliness matter

notes.text: Core distinction

Raw telemetry is an observation. An indicator is a representation intended to identify potentially relevant activity. Intelligence adds context, analytic judgment, provenance, confidence, relevance, and a consumer-specific implication or action.

items: Tactical intelligence supports near-term technical operations such as detection, investigation, and blocking decisions.
Operational intelligence explains activity patterns, campaigns, infrastructure, capabilities, and likely near-term adversary behavior.
Strategic intelligence informs risk, priorities, investment, and longer-term defensive decisions.

notes.text: An indicator is not automatically malicious. Shared infrastructure, dynamic addressing, common services, and benign prevalence can make a raw indicator ambiguous.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes cyber threat intelligence?
options: A list of every IP observed on the Internet
Analyzed and contextualized threat information used to support decisions
quiz.answer: Analyzed and contextualized threat information used to support decisions
quiz.explanation: Threat intelligence adds analysis and context so a consumer can make a defensible decision.

summary: Threat intelligence is decision-oriented, not a feed-size competition.
The meaning of an indicator depends on context and evidence.

lessons.title: The Intelligence Lifecycle
lessons.description: Use a lifecycle that moves from requirements to collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, and feedback.

notes.text: Lifecycle

items: Direction: define the question, consumer, decision, scope, and time horizon.
Collection: obtain relevant external and internal information.
Processing: normalize, deduplicate, timestamp, tag, and preserve provenance.
Analysis: assess reliability, relevance, relationships, confidence, and implications.
Dissemination: provide an actionable product to the appropriate audience with handling guidance.
Feedback: capture usefulness, sightings, corrections, and new requirements.

notes.text: The lifecycle is iterative rather than a rigid one-way pipeline. Feedback can change sources, collection priorities, analytic methods, and product formats.

practicals.title: Write an Intelligence Requirement
practicals.description: Turn a vague request into a usable intelligence requirement and collection plan.
steps: Define the consumer and decision.
Set a time horizon and priority.
List external source categories plus one internal validation source.
Define two measures that indicate the intelligence was useful.
practicals.solution:
import json

requirement = {
    "consumer": "SOC and vulnerability-management leads",
    "decision": "prioritize monitoring and remediation of exposed services",
    "time_horizon": "next 30 days",
    "sources": ["CISA KEV", "vendor advisories", "asset inventory", "internal security telemetry"],
    "validation": "Compare reported products and versions with owned assets.",
    "success_measures": ["Actionable findings are tied to owned assets.", "Every finding preserves provenance and confidence."]
}
print(json.dumps(requirement, indent=2))
practicals.output: Expected result: a bounded requirement that a collection and analysis process can actually answer.

summary: Begin with the question or decision that intelligence must support.
Feedback is part of intelligence operations, not an optional afterthought.

lessons.title: Actors, Campaigns, TTPs, and Attribution
lessons.description: Develop behavior-centered vocabulary and disciplined attribution habits.
learningObjectives: differentiate groups, campaigns, software, tools, tactics, and techniques

notes.text: MITRE ATT&CK models adversary behavior using tactics, techniques, and sub-techniques. ATT&CK Group pages describe activity clusters based on publicly reported information and encourage analysts to perform additional research.

items: Use behavior and evidence as the primary description.
Record aliases as source context; an alias is not proof of exact identity.
Shared tools, common hosting, and reused infrastructure can support multiple hypotheses.

notes.text: Attribution should be written as an evidence-weighted hypothesis rather than certainty from one indicator or one tool.

quiz.question: Why is one commonly used tool weak attribution evidence?
options: Multiple actors can use the same tool or native utility
quiz.answer: Multiple actors can use the same tool or native utility
quiz.explanation: Tool use overlaps across actors and defenders, so it is one evidence point rather than a unique identity marker.

summary: Behavioral descriptions are often more durable than actor labels.
Attribution confidence should rise only as independent evidence converges.

lessons.title: Source Evaluation and Collection Strategy
lessons.description: Evaluate source quality and build collection that serves defined intelligence requirements.
learningObjectives: compare reliability, relevance, timeliness, precision, and cost
identify blind spots and feed risks

items: Government/CERT advisories: useful for authoritative guidance and exploited-vulnerability reporting.
Vendor research: often rich in technical detail but varies in methodology and scope.
Community sharing: broad collaboration with a higher need for validation and provenance.
Internal sources: incidents, detections, telemetry, asset inventory, and investigations provide environmental relevance.

notes.text: Source scorecard

items: Requirement fit
Source reliability and provenance
Timeliness/update cadence
Precision/noise
Coverage and blind spots
Licensing/distribution constraints
Operational cost

quiz.question: Which factor best predicts whether a CTI source is operationally useful?
options: Fit to a defined requirement plus acceptable reliability and timeliness
quiz.answer: Fit to a defined requirement plus acceptable reliability and timeliness
quiz.explanation: Operational value comes from usefulness to a consumer and decision, supported by trustworthy and timely evidence.

summary: Choose sources because they answer requirements, not because they publish large feeds.
Review source performance periodically.

tasks.title: Build a Source Evaluation Matrix
tasks.description: Rank four sources against an intelligence requirement using explicit criteria.
tasks.problemStatement: A team needs intelligence about exploited vulnerabilities affecting internet-facing services. Score four supplied source records and document the recommendation.
tasks.hint: Use a weighted sum and make lower noise score better.
tasks.solutionCode:
sources = [
    {"name":"CISA KEV","relevance":5,"provenance":5,"timeliness":4,"noise":1},
    {"name":"Vendor bulletin","relevance":5,"provenance":4,"timeliness":4,"noise":2},
    {"name":"Broad IOC feed","relevance":2,"provenance":3,"timeliness":3,"noise":5},
    {"name":"Internal asset inventory","relevance":5,"provenance":5,"timeliness":5,"noise":1},
]
weights = {"relevance":0.40,"provenance":0.25,"timeliness":0.25,"noise":0.10}

def score(s):
    return (s["relevance"]*weights["relevance"] +
            s["provenance"]*weights["provenance"] +
            s["timeliness"]*weights["timeliness"] +
            (6-s["noise"])*weights["noise"])

for value, name in sorted(((score(s),s["name"]) for s in sources), reverse=True):
    print(f"{name}: {value:.2f}")
tasks.solutionExplanation: This score is a decision aid, not an objective truth; the weights must be documented and may differ by requirement.

modules.title: Indicators, Observables, and Context
modules.description: Teach indicator handling, normalization, lifecycle, and disciplined enrichment.

lessons.title: Indicators, Observables, and IoCs
lessons.description: Learn common indicator types and the difference between observable facts and analytic indicators.
learningObjectives: classify IPs, domains, URLs, hashes, email artifacts, and behavioral indicators
identify why a single indicator may be ambiguous

items: IPv4 addresses can be shared, dynamic, or infrastructure-related.
Domains and URLs can be precise but may change rapidly.
File hashes identify exact artifacts well but are brittle when files change.
Email artifacts gain value when sender, reply-to, URLs, attachments, authentication results, and timing are considered together.
Behavioral indicators describe patterns rather than one static value.

notes.text: An IoC list without provenance, timestamps, or validation can generate false positives and unsafe automation.

practicals.title: Normalize and Classify Mixed Indicators
practicals.description: Build a small classifier that normalizes training indicators and labels their type.
steps: Create inputs containing an IPv4 address, domain, URL, SHA-256 hash, and email.
Validate basic syntax.
Normalize domains and hashes to lowercase and preserve original values.
Print the type plus normalized value.
practicals.output: Expected result: each training value is classified and normalized while the original input remains available.

summary: Use indicator type and context to judge appropriate action.
Preserve original values when normalizing.

lessons.title: Confidence, Freshness, and Indicator Lifecycle
lessons.description: Design records that express confidence, timing, review, and expiration.
learningObjectives: separate source reliability from indicator confidence
explain why stale intelligence should stop influencing active controls

items: Source reliability describes trust in the producer or collection method.
Indicator confidence describes how strongly current evidence supports a claim.
Freshness affects usefulness and should be represented with observation and review timestamps.
Expiration or review dates should stop stale data from remaining active indefinitely.

notes.text: Retention and active-use lifecycle are different decisions: historical records may need retention even after an indicator is no longer active.

quiz.question: Why is freshness important for many indicators?
options: Indicators can change meaning or become stale
Freshness removes the need for validation
quiz.answer: Indicators can change meaning or become stale
quiz.explanation: Operational controls should account for how quickly intelligence can age or lose relevance.

summary: Confidence and freshness answer different questions.
Lifecycle metadata makes automation safer and auditable.

lessons.title: Enrichment and Pivoting
lessons.description: Move from one observable to related evidence while retaining provenance and avoiding unjustified conclusions.
learningObjectives: select pivots based on an investigation question
separate enrichment facts from analytic inference

notes.text: Pivot examples

items: Domain → DNS history → related names → certificates → hosting/infrastructure context.
Hash → artifact metadata → signing → malware relationships → internal sightings.
IP → ownership/hosting → domains → certificates → temporal activity.
Behavior → ATT&CK technique → needed data components → available telemetry.

notes.text: Enrichment results should include provider, retrieval time, and interpretation. A pivot creates a hypothesis; it does not automatically validate it.

practicals.title: Build an Enrichment Record
practicals.description: Create a JSON record that traces two synthetic pivots and explicitly separates facts from inference.
steps: Use example.org and 203.0.113.10 only as documentation-safe training values.
Record both pivots as synthetic.
Add a low-confidence inference that shared relationships do not prove maliciousness or attribution.
practicals.output: Expected result: a traceable enrichment chain that preserves provenance and uncertainty.

summary: Every pivot should have a purpose tied to the intelligence question.
Record provenance at the point of enrichment.

tasks.title: Implement Indicator Aging
tasks.description: Determine whether an indicator is active, due for review, expired, or invalid.
tasks.problemStatement: Build a timezone-aware status function using valid_from, valid_until, and review_at.
tasks.hint: Normalize a trailing Z to +00:00 before parsing.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The function uses UTC-aware timestamps and keeps review status distinct from expiration.

modules.title: STIX, TAXII, and Structured Sharing
modules.description: Teach interoperable CTI representation, exchange protocols, handling markings, and practical platform concepts.

lessons.title: STIX 2.1 Core Model
lessons.description: Understand the STIX graph model and the difference among indicators, observations, relationships, sightings, and bundles.
learningObjectives: distinguish indicators, observed data, and sightings

notes.text: STIX uses STIX Domain Objects and STIX Cyber-observable Objects as graph nodes, with Relationship Objects providing edges. A bundle packages STIX content.

items: Indicator: a pattern intended to detect potentially relevant activity.
Observed Data: observed cyber observables used as evidence.
Sighting: records that an intelligence entity was seen and can connect intelligence to where/when it was observed.
Relationship: typed links such as indicates connect related objects.

practicals.title: Create a Minimal STIX Bundle
practicals.description: Construct a small STIX 2.1 bundle with synthetic training data.
steps: Generate UUIDv4 values.
Create an indicator with a STIX pattern over a synthetic SHA-256 value.
Create a synthetic malware object and an indicates relationship.
Wrap objects in a bundle and parse the JSON.
practicals.output: Expected result: parseable JSON following the STIX 2.1 object/relationship model using explicitly synthetic data.

summary: STIX is a content model, not a truth oracle.
Relationships preserve context that flat indicator lists lose.

lessons.title: TAXII 2.1 Exchange Concepts
lessons.description: Learn discovery, API roots, collections, objects, status, pagination, and secure transport considerations.
learningObjectives: identify security and operational concerns for real deployments

items: Discovery exposes available API roots.
An API root exposes collections and related resources.
Collections store or provide CTI objects.
Servers can expose status for asynchronous processing.
Clients should handle pagination, content negotiation, authentication failures, rate limits, and transport errors.

notes.text: OASIS’s Medallion repository is explicitly a prototype/reference implementation and is not intended for production use; production deployments require appropriate authentication, authorization, TLS, hardening, logging, and operational controls.

quiz.question: What is the role of TAXII relative to STIX?
options: TAXII is the data model and STIX is the transport
TAXII defines exchange protocol semantics while STIX represents CTI content
quiz.answer: TAXII defines exchange protocol semantics while STIX represents CTI content
quiz.explanation: STIX provides the threat-information representation, while TAXII defines RESTful mechanisms for exchanging it.

summary: TAXII transports CTI; STIX represents the content.
A protocol standard does not remove operational security requirements.

lessons.title: TLP 2.0 and Controlled Sharing
lessons.description: Use Traffic Light Protocol markings correctly and understand their limits.
learningObjectives: differentiate the four TLP labels at a high level
separate handling markings from access control and legal classification

notes.text: FIRST’s Traffic Light Protocol facilitates controlled sharing of sensitive information. TLP 2.0 replaced earlier TLP versions as of 1 January 2023.

items: TLP:RED: recipients should not share outside the specific exchange context.
TLP:AMBER: restricted sharing to help recipients act, under the standard’s conditions.
TLP:GREEN: limited sharing within a community or sector.
TLP:CLEAR: broad sharing is permitted subject to applicable rules and copyright.

notes.text: TLP communicates sharing expectations. It does not itself enforce technical access controls or replace law, contract, privacy policy, or internal data classification.

quiz.question: What does TLP primarily communicate?
options: How sensitive information may be shared
quiz.answer: How sensitive information may be shared
quiz.explanation: TLP is a sharing and handling convention, not a truth or maliciousness rating.

summary: Apply TLP as a handling instruction.
Keep handling markings with the intelligence record through downstream workflows.

lessons.title: MISP and OpenCTI as CTI Platforms
lessons.description: Understand platform capabilities without confusing tooling with intelligence tradecraft.
learningObjectives: identify when platform automation should be governed carefully

notes.text: MISP provides workflows around sharing, events, attributes, taxonomies, galaxies, objects, warning lists, and APIs. OpenCTI is designed as a knowledge-graph platform for organizing and linking threat intelligence, observables, vulnerabilities, sightings, alerts, and related context.
A CTI platform stores and automates intelligence workflows; it does not replace source evaluation, analytic judgment, or governance.

summary: Choose a platform based on workflow, integrations, sharing, scale, and operational constraints.
Tool capability should not be mistaken for intelligence quality.

tasks.title: Validate a STIX Relationship Graph
tasks.description: Detect dangling STIX relationship references inside a bundle.
tasks.problemStatement: A received bundle contains indicators, malware, and relationships. Report relationships whose source_ref or target_ref is absent from the bundle.
tasks.hint: Build an ID set before validating relationships.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The validator checks structural graph integrity only; it does not establish whether the underlying intelligence claim is true.

modules.title: Threat Analysis and ATT&CK-Based Context
modules.description: Develop behavior-centered analysis, clustering, hypotheses, confidence, and vulnerability intelligence skills.

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK for CTI Analysts
lessons.description: Use ATT&CK to describe adversary behavior, communicate hypotheses, and reason about required telemetry.
learningObjectives: map observed behavior to ATT&CK concepts
use ATT&CK without treating it as an attribution engine

notes.text: ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Tactics describe why an action is performed; techniques describe how a tactical goal is achieved.
ATT&CK mappings must be evidence-based. Technique mapping does not prove attribution and does not automatically prove that an organization can detect that technique.

quiz.question: In ATT&CK, what do tactics represent?
options: Why the adversary performs an action
quiz.answer: Why the adversary performs an action
quiz.explanation: ATT&CK defines tactics as adversary goals or reasons for performing actions.

summary: ATT&CK provides a common behavioral language.
Detection coverage requires actual telemetry and analytics.

lessons.title: Campaign and Infrastructure Clustering
lessons.description: Combine infrastructure, artifact, timing, targeting, and behavior evidence into defensible clusters.
learningObjectives: build an evidence table for clustering
avoid false conclusions from shared infrastructure

items: Infrastructure: domains, IPs, certificates, hosting, naming patterns.
Artifacts: hashes, file metadata, configurations, filenames.
Behavior: ATT&CK techniques and distinctive execution/persistence patterns.
Time: first/last-seen patterns, turnover, campaign windows.
Targeting: sectors or technologies only when supported by evidence.

notes.text: Common hosting, CDNs, compromised servers, and legitimate shared services can connect unrelated activity. Cross-check with independent dimensions.

summary: Corroborate clusters across multiple independent evidence types.
State alternative explanations for ambiguous overlaps.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing and Confidence
lessons.description: Apply structured analytic thinking to avoid confirmation bias and make uncertainty explicit.
learningObjectives: score supporting and contradicting evidence transparently
identify what evidence would change the conclusion

items: State the question and decision.
List at least two plausible hypotheses.
Classify each evidence item as supporting, contradicting, or neutral.
Weight evidence by reliability or specificity when appropriate.
Record disconfirming evidence and missing information.
Publish confidence with caveats.

notes.text: An ordinal confidence label such as low/medium/high is not automatically a probability. Define what the scale means.

practicals.title: Build an Evidence Matrix
practicals.description: Evaluate two competing hypotheses about synthetic infrastructure relationships.
steps: Create H1: same campaign and H2: unrelated shared infrastructure.
Enter four synthetic evidence items with reliability and directional effects.
Calculate weighted directional scores.
Write a conditional conclusion and identify one missing data point.
practicals.solution:
evidence=[
 {"item":"overlapping malware configuration","reliability":4,"h1":1,"h2":-1},
 {"item":"same certificate pattern","reliability":3,"h1":1,"h2":-1},
 {"item":"same hosting provider","reliability":2,"h1":0,"h2":1},
 {"item":"different registration timing","reliability":2,"h1":-1,"h2":1},
]

h1=sum(e["reliability"]*e["h1"] for e in evidence)
h2=sum(e["reliability"]*e["h2"] for e in evidence)
print({"H1_score":h1,"H2_score":h2})
print("Scores are a reasoning aid, not a probability model.")
practicals.output: Expected result: a transparent analytic record that shows competing explanations rather than hiding uncertainty.

summary: Good analysis records how conclusions could be falsified.
Confidence should reflect evidence quality, not analyst certainty alone.

lessons.title: Vulnerability Intelligence and Exploitation Context
lessons.description: Use exploited-vulnerability information with exposure and asset context.
learningObjectives: distinguish a published vulnerability from exploitation evidence
use CISA KEV as one prioritization input
combine vulnerability intelligence with asset and business context

notes.text: CISA describes the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog as an authoritative source of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild and recommends using it as an input to vulnerability-management prioritization.

items: A vulnerable asset is not the same as a compromised asset.
Exploitation in the wild is not proof of exploitation in your environment.
Exposure, asset criticality, compensating controls, reachability, remediation options, and business impact still matter.

notes.text: Do not convert a CVE or KEV entry directly into an incident conclusion without local evidence.

summary: Threat intelligence can prioritize investigation and remediation questions.
Keep public exploitation evidence distinct from local compromise evidence.

tasks.title: Map Behavior to ATT&CK Evidence
tasks.description: Map observed behavior to ATT&CK and specify telemetry needed for confirmation.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a small report with technique IDs, rationale, confidence, and missing telemetry.
tasks.hint: Verify each ID against the ATT&CK release used by your organization.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The pattern explicitly records technique mapping, confidence, and telemetry gaps as separate analytic fields.

modules.title: Operational CTI: Hunting, Detection, and Sharing
modules.description: Teach how to turn intelligence into defensible detection, hunting, and sharing workflows.

lessons.title: From Intelligence to Detection Requirements
lessons.description: Translate intelligence into testable detection requirements instead of blindly importing feeds into controls.
learningObjectives: convert threat reporting into detection hypotheses
specify telemetry, validation, and false-positive conditions

items: Inform: briefings, watchlists, analyst notes.
Detect: rules, queries, correlation, analytics.
Hunt: hypotheses that guide targeted searches.
Prevent: block or control changes when confidence and safety justify them.
Respond: evidence-backed containment or remediation.

notes.text: Prevention has a different risk tolerance from detection. Always validate indicators and behavior before automated blocking.

summary: Operationalization should specify threat behavior, telemetry, logic, false positives, and validation.
Indicators can be one input among several signals.

lessons.title: Threat Hunting from Intelligence
lessons.description: Build scoped, falsifiable hunting hypotheses and report negative findings responsibly.

notes.text: Hunt structure

items: Hypothesis: a falsifiable statement.
Scope: users, assets, identities, time, cloud accounts, or network segments.
Telemetry: data needed to evaluate the hypothesis.
Query/analytic: the test applied to the data.
Outcome: confirmed, refuted, inconclusive, or telemetry insufficient.

notes.text: No results are not automatically evidence of absence. Missing logs, retention gaps, parser problems, or wrong assumptions can produce empty results.

practicals.title: Convert a Threat Report into a Hunt Plan
practicals.description: Turn a fictional intelligence statement into a scoped hunting plan.
steps: Use the hypothesis: a compromised privileged account may access an unusual internal service after successful authentication.
Define time window, identities, telemetry, query logic, and outcomes.
List two false positives.
Define escalation evidence.
practicals.solution:
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
import json

@dataclass
class HuntSpecification:
    hypothesis: str
    scope: str
    telemetry: list[str]
    logic: list[str]
    outcomes: list[str]
    false_positives: list[str]
    escalation: str

spec = HuntSpecification(
    hypothesis="A compromised privileged identity may access an unusual internal service after authentication.",
    scope="14 days; privileged identities; remote-access entry points",
    telemetry=["identity authentication", "VPN/remote access", "network connections", "asset inventory"],
    logic=["Find successful authentication.", "Join to service access in a bounded time window.", "Compare the destination with the approved baseline."],
    outcomes=["suspicious", "benign explained", "inconclusive", "telemetry insufficient"],
    false_positives=["emergency administration", "newly assigned responsibilities"],
    escalation="Escalate unexplained privileged access only when corroborating evidence supports the hypothesis."
)
print(json.dumps(asdict(spec), indent=2))
practicals.output: Expected result: a falsifiable hunt plan with explicit evidence requirements.

summary: Hunts should be bounded and testable.
Negative findings should include data-coverage limitations.

lessons.title: Sigma Detection Concepts
lessons.description: Use Sigma-style vendor-neutral detection logic and understand field mappings and backend conversion.
learningObjectives: explain why backend field mapping matters

items: logsource describes source assumptions.
detection contains selections and Boolean conditions.
Metadata such as title, description, level, status, falsepositives, and tags improves maintainability.
ATT&CK tags provide context; they do not prove coverage.

notes.text: Sigma rules still require target-platform field mappings and representative event testing. A Sigma rule is not automatically executable by every SIEM.

practicals.title: Write a Safe Sigma Training Rule
practicals.description: Create a benign training rule for a rare parent-child process relationship.
steps: Use synthetic Windows process-creation fields.
Match a browser parent launching Python as the child process.
Add an explicit false-positive note.
Keep the rule labeled experimental.
practicals.solution:
from pathlib import Path

sigma_yaml = r'''title: Rare browser-to-Python process relationship (training)
status: experimental
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - "\\browser.exe"
    Image|endswith:
      - "\\python.exe"
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Approved developer or test automation activity
level: medium
'''

Path("training_sigma_rule.yml").write_text(sigma_yaml, encoding="utf-8")
print("Wrote training_sigma_rule.yml")
practicals.output: Expected result: a readable vendor-neutral training rule that is explicitly subject to testing and tuning.

summary: Portability depends on semantic field mapping, not just syntax.
Validate rules against realistic event samples before production.

lessons.title: Intelligence Sharing and Feedback
lessons.description: Build sharing-ready products with provenance, confidence, handling markings, and an explicit feedback mechanism.
learningObjectives: request sightings, corrections, and other feedback

items: What happened?
Why does it matter?
What evidence supports the claim?
What is the confidence?
What can the recipient do now?
What handling/distribution rule applies?
How should sightings or corrections be returned?

notes.text: Sharing quality is measured by recipient action and feedback—not by the number of recipients or indicators transmitted.

summary: A good sharing product is actionable and traceable.
Feedback closes the loop and improves future intelligence.

tasks.title: Create a Hunt-to-Detection Specification
tasks.description: Produce a portable detection specification from a hunt hypothesis.
tasks.problemStatement: A detection engineer needs a reviewable specification before implementing a query in a particular SIEM.
tasks.hint: Keep the hypothesis separate from vendor-specific query syntax.
tasks.solutionCode:
import json
spec={
 "title":"Unusual privileged authentication followed by sensitive-service access",
 "hypothesis":"A privileged identity may be compromised when successful authentication is followed by unexplained access to a sensitive service.",
 "telemetry":["identity_authentication","remote_access","network_connection","asset_inventory"],
 "logic":["find successful privileged authentication","join to service access in a bounded time window","compare destination to approved baseline","require corroborating evidence before escalation"],
 "attck":["T1078"],
 "false_positives":["approved emergency administration","new responsibilities"],
 "validation":["replay benign events","replay controlled suspicious test events","measure precision","check telemetry coverage"],
 "tuning":["scope to high-value identities","maintain approved exceptions","require supporting signals"]
}
print(json.dumps(spec,indent=2))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The specification is portable because it separates the analytic hypothesis, data dependencies, and validation from a particular SIEM query language.

modules.title: CTI Program Operations and Quality
modules.description: Operate a sustainable intelligence capability with governance, metrics, source controls, and incident feedback.

lessons.title: Governance, Privacy, and Handling
lessons.description: Design CTI governance for access, purpose, provenance, privacy, retention, and controlled sharing.
learningObjectives: separate TLP handling from technical permissions

items: Purpose: why is the data collected?
Access: who needs it and at what sensitivity?
Provenance: where did it originate?
Handling: what sharing limits apply?
Retention: what remains historically useful and what should stop active use?
Privacy: does it contain personal or sensitive information?

notes.text: CTI may contain victim information, personal data, credentials, or other sensitive content. Apply applicable policy and legal requirements and minimize unnecessary collection.

summary: Governance is part of operational quality and safety.
TLP does not enforce access control by itself.

lessons.title: CTI Metrics and Quality Assurance
lessons.description: Measure CTI by its usefulness and security outcomes rather than feed volume.

items: Timeliness: time from publication to usable intelligence.
Actionability: intelligence leading to a documented defensive action or decision.
Precision: proportion of operationalized intelligence that remains relevant after validation.
Coverage: alignment with intelligence requirements and key assets.
Feedback: sightings, corrections, and information gaps.
Lifecycle: stale active intelligence removed or reviewed on time.

notes.text: Metrics can be gamed. Large indicator counts or alert volumes can represent noise rather than success.

summary: Connect metrics to decisions and outcomes.
Combine quantitative metrics with analyst and consumer feedback.

lessons.title: Source and Feed Risk Management
lessons.description: Protect CTI pipelines against malformed content, poisoning, drift, schema changes, outages, and licensing problems.

items: Validate schemas and field types before ingestion.
Quarantine malformed or unexpected updates.
Monitor volume, duplicates, missing fields, and timestamp drift.
Track licensing and redistribution requirements.
Keep source-specific trust and rollback controls.

notes.text: An external feed can influence security controls. Treat feed changes as operational events that require monitoring and review.

summary: External intelligence dependencies deserve supply-chain controls.
Automated enforcement should require a validated path from source to action.

lessons.title: Incident Integration and Feedback Loops
lessons.description: Connect CTI with incident response and feed validated incident findings back into intelligence.
learningObjectives: capture validated new indicators and TTPs
return lessons and observations into future intelligence

notes.text: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 was finalized in April 2025 and supersedes Revision 2. It places incident response recommendations throughout the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 risk-management approach.

items: CTI can enrich incident artifacts, identify related activity, and support response decisions.
Incident findings can produce new indicators, behavior observations, and intelligence requirements.
Evidence and intelligence claims should remain linked but conceptually distinct.

notes.text: Do not publish unvalidated incident details. Preserve evidence handling, authorization, privacy, and provenance before external sharing.

summary: Incident response can generate new intelligence as well as consume it.
Keep evidence provenance intact through analytic and sharing workflows.

tasks.title: Design a CTI Data-Quality Gate
tasks.description: Build an ingestion validator for required CTI fields and handling controls.
tasks.problemStatement: Reject records with missing provenance, unsupported TLP, invalid confidence, malformed timestamps, or future observations.
objectives: validate timestamp format and time direction
tasks.hint: Return all validation findings instead of failing on the first error.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The validator creates a safety boundary before data reaches downstream controls. Production deployments should add organization-specific policies and authorization requirements.

modules.title: Capstone: Threat Intelligence Fusion and Prioritization Pipeline
modules.description: Final practical assessment that combines collection context, indicator handling, structured CTI, ATT&CK context, sharing controls, quality checks, and prioritization in one reproducible local project.

lessons.title: Capstone Implementation and Assessment
lessons.description: Assemble the complete pipeline and evaluate it against course concepts.
learningObjectives: explain each stage and its assumptions
validate output and defend prioritization decisions

notes.text: Assessment focus

items: Data quality and provenance
Safe handling and lifecycle logic
Reasoning transparency
ATT&CK context without over-claiming
Actionable output for a consumer

summary: The capstone integrates the course as a workflow rather than a collection of isolated concepts.
A good result is reproducible, explainable, and appropriately cautious.

project.name: CTI Fusion and Prioritization Pipeline
project.description: A local vendor-neutral Python project that ingests synthetic intelligence observations, validates them, normalizes and deduplicates indicators, applies transparent confidence/freshness/actionability scoring, preserves TLP and provenance, attaches local ATT&CK context, and produces a Markdown intelligence brief. It deliberately avoids live enrichment, external network access, and automatic blocking so students can concentrate on safe, auditable intelligence tradecraft.
steps: Create app.py and the input directory.
Use synthetic training observations only; documentation-safe example values are provided.
Run the built-in self-test before changing the pipeline.
Run the pipeline against input/observations.json.
Inspect validation failures and correct the data rather than bypassing checks.
Review the deduplicated prioritized report and verify provenance, handling, context, and next actions.
Adapt the scoring weights only with documented analytic justification.
For production use, add real source authentication, authorization, licensing controls, external-service error handling, caching, schema validation, monitoring, and organization-specific policy.

input/observations.json.context: Second synthetic source used to exercise deduplication.

project.explanation: Architecture: local JSON observations enter a validation layer, then normalization and deduplication, transparent priority scoring, local ATT&CK context lookup, and Markdown rendering. Each stage preserves provenance and explicit uncertainty. The project demonstrates an end-to-end CTI workflow without live lookups or automated enforcement, which makes it reproducible and safe for student use.

currentPracticeNotes: MITRE ATT&CK Data Sources were deprecated in the ATT&CK v18 release; the course uses current Data Components rather than teaching Data Sources as the modern model.
